claim: The suspended microchannel resonator (SMR) is capable of measuring buoyant mass of single cells with a precision of <0.1 pg.
source: SMR is a microfluidic cantilever that is capable of measuring buoyant mass (a proxy of dry mass, referred to as mass from here on) of single cells with a precision of <0.1 pg (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–d) (Burg et al., 2007; Son et al., 2015a; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Burg et al., 2007; Son et al., 2015a; Son et al., 2012) and references to figures showing the measurement precision.

claim: The SMR measurement precision of <0.1 pg corresponds to <8 nm (<0.07%) change in a spherical lymphocyte cell diameter.
source: This resolution corresponds to <8 nm (<0.07%) change in a spherical lymphocyte cell diameter.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measurement precision stated in the manuscript.

claim: L1210 mouse lymphocytes accumulate on average 12% of their total cell cycle mass during M-phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).
source: In total, we analyzed 180 individual L1210 cells undergoing mitosis and observed that on average 12% of the total mass accumulated during the whole cell cycle was acquired during M-phase (i.e. during mitosis and cytokinesis) (Figure 1d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from 180 individual cells shown in Figure 1d.

claim: L1210 cells accumulate 7% of total cell growth during early mitosis (before metaphase-to-anaphase transition).
source: 7% of total cell growth took place during early mitosis, while 5% took place during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the SMR data on L1210 cells.

claim: L1210 cells accumulate 5% of total cell growth during cytokinesis (after metaphase-to-anaphase transition).
source: 7% of total cell growth took place during early mitosis, while 5% took place during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the SMR data on L1210 cells.

claim: Mass accumulation during anaphase is negligible.
source: During anaphase, duration of which was estimated based on cell elongation (Materials and methods), mass accumulation was negligible.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements.

claim: M-phase lasts approximately 10% of the whole cell cycle in most cell lines.
source: Considering that in most cell lines M-phase lasts approximately 10% of the whole cell cycle, the 12% mass accumulation observed during M-phase makes M-phase growth comparable to interphase growth.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about cell cycle timing.

claim: The 12% mass accumulation during M-phase makes M-phase growth comparable to interphase growth.
source: Considering that in most cell lines M-phase lasts approximately 10% of the whole cell cycle, the 12% mass accumulation observed during M-phase makes M-phase growth comparable to interphase growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative duration of M-phase and the amount of growth observed.

claim: Mouse FL5.12 and BaF3 pro-B lymphocytes grow 9–13% of their total mass in M-phase.
source: Mouse FL5.12 and BaF3 pro-B lymphocytes, and chicken DT40 lymphoblasts grew 9–13% of their total mass in M-phase (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly measured data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Chicken DT40 lymphoblasts grow 9–13% of their total mass in M-phase.
source: Mouse FL5.12 and BaF3 pro-B lymphocytes, and chicken DT40 lymphoblasts grew 9–13% of their total mass in M-phase (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly measured data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Suspension HeLa (S-HeLa) cells grow 14% of their total mass during M-phase.
source: Suspension HeLa (S-HeLa) cells also grew 14% of their total mass during M-phase, validating that substantial growth in M-phase is not specific to lymphocytes.
evidence: This is directly measured data from S-HeLa cells.

claim: Substantial growth in M-phase is not specific to lymphocytes.
source: Suspension HeLa (S-HeLa) cells also grew 14% of their total mass during M-phase, validating that substantial growth in M-phase is not specific to lymphocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both lymphocytes and HeLa cells show substantial M-phase growth.

claim: CD3+ and CD8+ activated primary human T cells add approximately 7% of their total mass during M-phase.
source: We also examined CD3 +and CD8+activated primary human T cells. Both T-cell subpopulations added approximately 7% of their total mass during M-phase.
evidence: This is directly measured data from primary human T cells.

claim: Growth in mitosis and cytokinesis is an important contributor to total cellular growth across a variety of cell types grown in suspension.
source: Thus, growth in mitosis and cytokinesis is an important contributor to the total cellular growth across a variety of cell types grown in suspension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing consistent M-phase growth across multiple cell types.

claim: After mitotic entry (during approximate prophase), L1210 cells exhibit on average 15.8 ± 3% (mean ± SEM, n = 180) increase in mass accumulation rate (MAR) when compared to late G2 phase.
source: Surprisingly, after mitotic entry (during approximate prophase) L1210 cells exhibited on average 15.8 ± 3% (mean ± SEM, n = 180) increase in MAR when compared to late G2 phase (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SMR data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: As L1210 cells approach the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, MAR rapidly decreases and eventually reaches zero at the end of metaphase.
source: As cells approached the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, MAR rapidly decreased and eventually reached zero at the end of metaphase.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements shown in Figure 2a.

claim: MAR remains near zero for the approximate duration of anaphase in L1210 cells.
source: MAR remained near zero for the approximate duration of anaphase, after which MAR started to recover during late cytokinesis (Figure 2a,c,d).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements.

claim: MAR starts to recover during late cytokinesis after anaphase in L1210 cells.
source: MAR remained near zero for the approximate duration of anaphase, after which MAR started to recover during late cytokinesis (Figure 2a,c,d).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements.

claim: The recovery of MAR continues through the abscission of daughter cells.
source: The recovery of MAR continued through the abscission of daughter cells (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Cell growth dynamics during mitosis persist under different nutrient conditions.
source: These cell growth dynamics also persisted under different nutrient conditions and were reproducible with different SMR devices over multiple years of study (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This is based on experiments conducted under different nutrient conditions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: Cell growth dynamics during mitosis are reproducible with different SMR devices over multiple years of study.
source: These cell growth dynamics also persisted under different nutrient conditions and were reproducible with different SMR devices over multiple years of study (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This is based on experiments conducted with different SMR devices over multiple years shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: All cell types studied display rapid reduction of MAR during metaphase (possibly starting in late prometaphase).
source: All cell types displayed rapid reduction of MAR during metaphase (possibly starting in late prometaphase), near zero MAR during anaphase and a recovery of MAR during late cytokinesis.
evidence: This is based on observations across multiple cell types shown in Figure 2e.

claim: All cell types studied display near zero MAR during anaphase.
source: All cell types displayed rapid reduction of MAR during metaphase (possibly starting in late prometaphase), near zero MAR during anaphase and a recovery of MAR during late cytokinesis.
evidence: This is based on observations across multiple cell types shown in Figure 2e.

claim: All cell types studied display a recovery of MAR during late cytokinesis.
source: All cell types displayed rapid reduction of MAR during metaphase (possibly starting in late prometaphase), near zero MAR during anaphase and a recovery of MAR during late cytokinesis.
evidence: This is based on observations across multiple cell types shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The temporary stop of cell growth in anaphase is consistently short (<15 min).
source: The temporary stop of cell growth in anaphase was consistently short (<15 min) and coincided with the physical separation of the daughter cells (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is based on timing measurements from SMR data shown in Figure 2c–e.

claim: The temporary stop of cell growth in anaphase coincides with the physical separation of the daughter cells.
source: The temporary stop of cell growth in anaphase was consistently short (<15 min) and coincided with the physical separation of the daughter cells (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is based on observations correlating growth cessation with cell separation shown in Figure 2c–e.

claim: Some cells display a negative MAR, indicating a small loss of cell mass during late metaphase and/or early anaphase.
source: Notably, some cells displayed a negative MAR, indicating a small loss of cell mass during late metaphase and/or early anaphase (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from SMR measurements shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The mitotic growth behavior is conserved across various animal cell types in suspension.
source: Together, these results indicate that the mitotic growth behavior is conserved across various animal cell types in suspension, suggesting a role for these specific growth dynamics during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar growth patterns across multiple cell types.

claim: The conserved mitotic growth behavior suggests a role for these specific growth dynamics during mitosis.
source: Together, these results indicate that the mitotic growth behavior is conserved across various animal cell types in suspension, suggesting a role for these specific growth dynamics during mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the conservation of growth patterns.

claim: Proteins constitute approximately 70% of cellular dry mass.
source: Proteins constitute approximately 70% of cellular dry mass (Palm and Thompson, 2017), making it likely that the measured MAR dynamics reflect protein synthesis rates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Palm and Thompson, 2017.

claim: The measured MAR dynamics likely reflect protein synthesis rates.
source: Proteins constitute approximately 70% of cellular dry mass (Palm and Thompson, 2017), making it likely that the measured MAR dynamics reflect protein synthesis rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that proteins constitute most of the dry mass.

claim: For unsynchronized L1210 cells, the average mitotic protein synthesis rates are 85 ± 6% (mean ± SD, n = 6) of the rate for G2 cells.
source: For unsynchronized cells, the average mitotic protein synthesis rates were 85 ± 6% (mean ± SD, n = 6) of the rate for G2 cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from OPP-based protein synthesis assays.

claim: Immediately after release from G2 arrest, when mitotic cells are in prophase, protein synthesis rates are higher in mitotic cells than in G2 cells.
source: Immediately after the release from G2 arrest, when mitotic cells were in prophase, protein synthesis rates were higher in mitotic cells than in G2 cells (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Approximately 30 min after release from G2 arrest, when most mitotic cells proceed to cytokinesis, protein synthesis rates are reduced to below the normal G2 levels.
source: Approximately 30 min later, when most mitotic cells proceeded to cytokinesis, the protein synthesis rates were reduced to below the normal G2 levels.
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements at different time points after G2 release.

claim: Early mitotic L1210 cells (prophase) have higher protein synthesis rates than G2 cells in the absence of cell cycle synchronization.
source: In the absence of cell cycle synchronization, OPP-based protein synthesis assay indicated that early mitotic cells have higher protein synthesis rates than G2 cells, whereas in late mitotic cells, protein synthesis is reduced (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements using Cyclin A to separate early and late mitotic cells, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In late mitotic L1210 cells (metaphase to telophase), protein synthesis is reduced compared to G2 cells.
source: In the absence of cell cycle synchronization, OPP-based protein synthesis assay indicated that early mitotic cells have higher protein synthesis rates than G2 cells, whereas in late mitotic cells, protein synthesis is reduced (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements using Cyclin A to separate early and late mitotic cells, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Protein synthesis rates remain high in early mitosis but not in late mitosis when cells are separated based on cyclin B1.
source: This approach also revealed that protein synthesis rates remain high in early mitosis but not in late mitosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements using cyclin B1 to separate mitotic stages, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: L1210 cells display increased growth in early mitosis and radically reduced growth in metaphase and anaphase.
source: In conclusion, L1210 cells display increased growth in early mitosis and radically reduced growth in metaphase and anaphase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on both MAR and protein synthesis measurements.

claim: L1210 cells treated with STLC (kinesin inhibitor) display a growth burst in early mitosis, similarly to untreated cells.
source: First, we monitored the MAR of L1210 cells treated with kinesin inhibitor S-trityl-l-cysteine (STLC), which arrests cells in prometaphase state. These cells displayed a growth burst in early mitosis, similarly to untreated cells, after which MAR approached zero over the course of 2–3 hr (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements of STLC-treated cells shown in Figure 4a.

claim: After the initial growth burst, MAR approaches zero over the course of 2–3 hr in STLC-treated L1210 cells arrested in prometaphase.
source: These cells displayed a growth burst in early mitosis, similarly to untreated cells, after which MAR approached zero over the course of 2–3 hr (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements of STLC-treated cells shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In STLC-treated L1210 cells, protein synthesis rates increase after mitotic entry, but then gradually decrease as cells are arrested in mitosis.
source: Similarly to MAR, protein synthesis rates increased after mitotic entry, but then gradually decreased as cells were arrested in mitosis (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in STLC-treated cells shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Nocodazole treatment results in identical MAR behavior as STLC in L1210 cells.
source: In addition, nocodazole treatment resulted in identical MAR behavior as STLC (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements comparing nocodazole and STLC treatments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Treatment with STLC, nocodazole, MG-132, and proTAME all result in similar reduction in overall mitotic protein synthesis.
source: All these chemicals resulted in similar reduction in the overall mitotic protein synthesis (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements with different mitotic arrest chemicals shown in Figure 4c.

claim: None of the mitotic arrest chemicals (STLC, nocodazole, proTAME) cause protein synthesis to be significantly reduced in G2, except for MG-132.
source: None of these chemicals caused protein synthesis to be significantly reduced in G2, except for MG-132.
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in G2 cells treated with different chemicals.

claim: Clinically relevant concentrations of Vinblastine and Vincristine do not affect cell growth in G2.
source: Neither of the drugs affected cell growth in G2, but as cells were arrested in mitosis, their growth rate reduced to zero (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in cells treated with Vinblastine and Vincristine shown in Figure 4d.

claim: As L1210 cells are arrested in mitosis by Vinblastine or Vincristine, their growth rate reduces to zero.
source: Neither of the drugs affected cell growth in G2, but as cells were arrested in mitosis, their growth rate reduced to zero (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in cells treated with Vinblastine and Vincristine shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Mitotic arrests stop cell growth independently of the arresting mechanism.
source: Thus, mitotic arrests, including antimitotic chemotherapies, stop cell growth independently of the arresting mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on observations with multiple different mitotic arrest mechanisms.

claim: Inhibition of mitotic swelling removes the MAR increase seen in early mitosis but does not affect MAR in metaphase and anaphase.
source: While mitotic rounding has minimal influence on the cell types used in this study, as the suspension cells display a spherical morphology throughout the cell cycle, inhibition of mitotic cell swelling removed the MAR increase seen in early mitosis but did not affect MAR in metaphase and anaphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in cells treated with EIPA to inhibit mitotic swelling, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: Inhibition of mitotic swelling does not influence early mitotic protein synthesis rates.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of mitotic swelling did not influence early mitotic protein synthesis rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in cells treated with EIPA shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Mitotic swelling influences the MAR observed in early mitosis, possibly by increasing cell mass due to the uptake of ions.
source: Thus, while mitotic swelling influences the MAR observed in early mitosis, possibly by increasing cell mass due to the uptake of ions, this does not explain why cells suddenly stop growing around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of inhibiting mitotic swelling on MAR.

claim: Mitotic swelling does not explain why cells suddenly stop growing around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: Thus, while mitotic swelling influences the MAR observed in early mitosis, possibly by increasing cell mass due to the uptake of ions, this does not explain why cells suddenly stop growing around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that inhibiting swelling doesn't affect MAR in metaphase/anaphase.

claim: Tozasertib-treated L1210 cells display low MAR around metaphase-to-anaphase transition, although MAR remains higher than in control cells.
source: Tozasertib-treated cells displayed low MAR around metaphase-to-anaphase transition, although MAR remained higher than in control cells (Figure 5b; Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in Tozasertib-treated cells shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment results in MAR dynamics comparable to control cells.
source: Blebbistatin treatment resulted in MAR dynamics comparable to control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in blebbistatin-treated cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Both Tozasertib and blebbistatin prolong the duration of early mitosis.
source: In addition, both Tozasertib and blebbistatin prolonged the duration of early mitosis.
evidence: This is based on observations from MAR measurements and imaging.

claim: The physical separation of daughter cells does not explain the observed MAR dynamics.
source: Together, these data indicate that the physical separation of daughter cells does not explain the observed MAR dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments blocking cytokinesis with Tozasertib and blebbistatin.

claim: 20 min after mitotic entry, control and STLC-treated L1210 cells display similar growth rates.
source: 20 min after mitotic entry, when cells are in late prometaphase, both samples displayed similar growth rates (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements comparing control and STLC-treated cells shown in Figure 5d.

claim: 28 min and 32 min after mitotic entry, control L1210 cells display lower MAR than STLC-treated cells arrested in prometaphase.
source: However, 28 min and 32 min after mitotic entry, when control cells had proceeded to metaphase and anaphase, respectively, but STLC-treated cells remained arrested in prometaphase, the control cells displayed lower MAR.
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements comparing control and STLC-treated cells at specific time points.

claim: The mitotic morphological changes and the time that cells have spent in mitosis cannot fully explain the observed MAR in metaphase and anaphase.
source: In conclusion, the mitotic morphological changes (Figure 5a,b; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b) and the time that cells have spent in mitosis cannot fully explain the observed MAR in metaphase and anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments comparing control and arrested cells.

claim: Additional MAR reducing mechanism(s) must exist around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: Thus, additional MAR reducing mechanism(s) must exist around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that time in mitosis alone doesn't explain MAR reduction.

claim: Phosphorylated 4E-BP1 (Thr37/46) levels are approximately threefold higher in mitosis than in G2 in L1210 cells.
source: Phosphorylated 4E-BP1 levels were approximately threefold higher in mitosis than in G2 (Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whereas phosphorylated S6RP displayed only a minor increase in mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on antibody staining and flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylated S6RP (Ser235/236) displays only a minor increase in mitosis compared to G2 in L1210 cells.
source: Phosphorylated 4E-BP1 levels were approximately threefold higher in mitosis than in G2 (Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whereas phosphorylated S6RP displayed only a minor increase in mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on antibody staining and flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The mitotic phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 is consistent with previous reports.
source: The mitotic phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 is also consistent with previous reports (Shuda et al., 2015) and the observation that the translational targets of mTOR are actively translated during mitosis (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Shuda et al., 2015; Park et al., 2016).

claim: The translational targets of mTOR are actively translated during mitosis.
source: The mitotic phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 is also consistent with previous reports (Shuda et al., 2015) and the observation that the translational targets of mTOR are actively translated during mitosis (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2016.

claim: TORIN-1 treatment reduces phosphorylated 4E-BP1 (Thr37/46) and S6RP (Ser235/236) levels to near zero in G2 L1210 cells.
source: In G2 cells, the levels of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 (Thr37/46) and S6RP (Ser235/236) were near zero (Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on measurements in TORIN-1 treated cells shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: TORIN-1 treatment reduces phosphorylation of S6RP in mitosis, indicating that mTOR remains active in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, phosphorylation of S6RP was reduced by TORIN-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b), indicating that mTOR remains active in mitosis.
evidence: This is based on measurements in TORIN-1 treated mitotic cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: TORIN-1 does not change the levels of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 in mitosis, suggesting that an mTOR-independent mechanism activates 4E-BP1 in mitosis.
source: However, TORIN-1 did not change the levels of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 in mitosis (Figure 6b), suggesting that an mTOR-independent mechanism activates 4E-BP1 in mitosis.
evidence: This is based on measurements in TORIN-1 treated mitotic cells shown in Figure 6b.

claim: TORIN-1 reduces G2 protein synthesis rates but does not affect mitotic protein synthesis rates.
source: Although G2 protein synthesis rates were reduced, mitotic protein synthesis rates were not affected by TORIN-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in TORIN-1 treated cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c.

claim: mTOR is not a major contributor to mitotic growth.
source: Thus, mTOR is not a major contributor to mitotic growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that TORIN-1 doesn't affect mitotic protein synthesis.

claim: RO-3306 (1 µM) reduces phosphorylated 4E-BP1 only in mitosis, not in G2.
source: Only in mitosis did RO-3306 reduce phosphorylated 4E-BP1 but not phosphorylated S6RP (Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on measurements in RO-3306 treated cells shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: RO-3306 (1 µM) does not reduce phosphorylated S6RP in mitosis.
source: Only in mitosis did RO-3306 reduce phosphorylated 4E-BP1 but not phosphorylated S6RP (Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on measurements in RO-3306 treated cells shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: RO-3306 (1 µM) treatment reduces mitotic protein synthesis rates without affecting G2 protein synthesis rates.
source: We observed that 1 µM RO-3306 treatment also reduced mitotic protein synthesis rates without affecting G2 protein synthesis rates (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in RO-3306 treated cells shown in Figure 6c.

claim: RO-3306 treatment prolongs early mitosis.
source: In addition, RO-3306 treatment prolonged early mitosis and resulted in a clear reduction of MAR in mitosis but not in G2 (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in RO-3306 treated cells shown in Figure 6d.

claim: RO-3306 treatment results in a clear reduction of MAR in mitosis but not in G2.
source: In addition, RO-3306 treatment prolonged early mitosis and resulted in a clear reduction of MAR in mitosis but not in G2 (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in RO-3306 treated cells shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In DT40 CDK1as cells, protein synthesis is reduced by 1NM-PP1 in a dose-dependent manner in mitosis but not in G2.
source: We observed that protein synthesis was reduced by 1NM-PP1 in a dose-dependent manner in mitosis but not in G2 (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in DT40 CDK1as cells treated with 1NM-PP1 shown in Figure 6e.

claim: 1NM-PP1 reduces MAR in mitosis in DT40 CDK1as cells.
source: Consistently, 1NM-PP1 also reduced MAR in mitosis (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in DT40 CDK1as cells treated with 1NM-PP1 shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Inhibitors for CDK2, Aurora kinases and DYRK kinases do not affect mitotic protein synthesis.
source: Inhibitors for CDK2, Aurora kinases and DYRK kinases did not affect mitotic protein synthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements with various kinase inhibitors shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a.

claim: OTSSP167 reduces phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, protein synthesis and mass accumulation rates in mitosis.
source: OTSSP167, a drug designated as a MELK inhibitor (Chung et al., 2012), reduced phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, protein synthesis and mass accumulation rates in mitosis (Figure 6b–d).
evidence: This is based on measurements in OTSSP167 treated cells shown in Figure 6b–d.

claim: Alternative MELK inhibitors do not display mitosis-specific inhibition of protein synthesis.
source: However, alternative MELK inhibitors (Klaeger et al., 2017) did not display mitosis-specific inhibition of protein synthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3b,c), suggesting that the mitotic growth effects observed in OTSSP167-treated cells were not mediated by MELK but by OTSSP167 off-targets.
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements with alternative MELK inhibitors shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3b,c.

claim: The mitotic growth effects observed in OTSSP167-treated cells are not mediated by MELK but by OTSSP167 off-targets.
source: However, alternative MELK inhibitors (Klaeger et al., 2017) did not display mitosis-specific inhibition of protein synthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3b,c), suggesting that the mitotic growth effects observed in OTSSP167-treated cells were not mediated by MELK but by OTSSP167 off-targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect with alternative MELK inhibitors.

claim: 4E-BP1 knockdown partially rescues mitotic protein synthesis inhibition caused by CDK1 inhibition with RO-3306.
source: However, when we reduced mitotic protein synthesis by inhibiting CDK1 with RO-3306, the knockdowns of 4E-BP1 partially rescued the mitotic protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in 4E-BP1 knockdown cells treated with RO-3306 shown in Figure 6g.

claim: CDK1 promotes mitotic growth at least partly through 4E-BP1.
source: These data indicate that CDK1 promotes mitotic growth at least partly through 4E-BP1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 4E-BP1 knockdown rescue experiments.

claim: Both G2 and mitotic protein synthesis rates are reduced by approximately 50% following 4EGI-1 treatment.
source: Both G2 and mitotic protein synthesis rates were reduced by a similar amount, approximately 50%, following 4EGI-1 treatment (Figure 6h).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in 4EGI-1 treated cells shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Treatment with both 4EGI-1 and RO-3306 does not significantly change mitotic protein synthesis rates when compared to treatment with 4EGI-1 alone.
source: However, treatment with both 4EGI-1 and RO-3306 did not significantly change mitotic protein synthesis rates when compared to treatment with 4EGI-1 alone, suggesting that cap-dependent protein synthesis is involved in CDK1-driven mitotic translation.
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements with combined 4EGI-1 and RO-3306 treatment.

claim: Cap-dependent protein synthesis is involved in CDK1-driven mitotic translation.
source: However, treatment with both 4EGI-1 and RO-3306 did not significantly change mitotic protein synthesis rates when compared to treatment with 4EGI-1 alone, suggesting that cap-dependent protein synthesis is involved in CDK1-driven mitotic translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of additive effect of 4EGI-1 and RO-3306.

claim: CDK1 substitutes for mTOR in mitosis to promote phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, to maintain cap-dependent translation and to promote mass accumulation.
source: In conclusion, our results are consistent with a previous report (Shuda et al., 2015) that CDK1 substitutes for mTOR in mitosis to promote phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, to maintain cap-dependent translation and to promote mass accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experiments and is consistent with previous work (Shuda et al., 2015).

claim: Following mitotic growth inhibition with RO-3306 or OTSSP167, G2 MAR is not affected, but MAR remains low in cytokinesis and in newborn G1.
source: In the presence of the mitotic growth inhibitors, G2 MAR was not affected, but MAR remained low in cytokinesis and in newborn G1 (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in cells treated with mitotic growth inhibitors shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Cells treated with 100 nM cycloheximide do not display similar cell cycle specificity in growth inhibition as cells treated with mitotic growth inhibitors.
source: In contrast, cells treated with 100 nM cycloheximide, a translation inhibitor which at this concentration reduces total protein synthesis by approximately 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), did not display similar cell cycle specificity in growth inhibition (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements comparing cycloheximide with mitotic growth inhibitors shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Mother cell MAR in early mitosis and daughter cell MAR in early G1 correlate in both control (R2 = 0.42) and RO-3306 (R2 = 0.33) treated cells.
source: In addition, mother cell MAR in early mitosis and daughter cell MAR in early G1 correlated in both control (R2 = 0.42) and RO-3306 (R2 = 0.33) treated cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1NM-PP1-mediated inhibition of CDK1 in the DT40 CDK1as cell line results in reduced growth during cytokinesis and in daughter cells.
source: 1NM-PP1-mediated inhibition of CDK1 in the DT40 CDK1as cell line also resulted in reduced growth during cytokinesis and in daughter cells (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is based on MAR measurements in DT40 CDK1as cells treated with 1NM-PP1 shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Following mitotic growth inhibitions, newborn cells display significantly reduced MAR and protein synthesis rates.
source: Following mitotic growth inhibitions, either by temporary mitotic arrest (4 hr STLC treatment) or by partial CDK1 inhibition, newborn cells displayed significantly reduced MAR and protein synthesis rates (Figure 7c,d; Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on MAR and protein synthesis measurements in daughter cells shown in Figure 7c,d and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: 4E-BP1 knockdown partly rescues daughter cell protein synthesis rates that were reduced by CDK1 inhibition.
source: 4E-BP1 knockdown partly rescued the daughter cell protein synthesis rates that were reduced by CDK1 inhibition (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is based on protein synthesis measurements in daughter cells from 4E-BP1 knockdown mothers shown in Figure 7e.

claim: 4E-BP1 mediates mitotic protein synthesis of CDK1, and this may also affect daughter cell protein synthesis.
source: Thus, 4E-BP1 mediates mitotic protein synthesis of CDK1 (Figure 6), and this may also affect daughter cell protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 4E-BP1 knockdown rescue experiments in daughter cells.

claim: The protein synthesis rate and long-term proliferation rate of daughter cells recover over time after mitotic growth inhibitions.
source: The protein synthesis rate and long-term proliferation rate of the daughter cells recovered over time (Figure 7e,f), suggesting that mitotic growth inhibitions do not permanently affect cell viability.
evidence: This is based on time-course measurements of protein synthesis and proliferation shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Mitotic growth inhibitions do not permanently affect cell viability.
source: The protein synthesis rate and long-term proliferation rate of the daughter cells recovered over time (Figure 7e,f), suggesting that mitotic growth inhibitions do not permanently affect cell viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the recovery of protein synthesis and proliferation over time.

claim: Animal cells grow approximately 10% of their total mass during M-phase.
source: We show that animal cells grow approximately 10% of their total mass during M-phase (Figure 1), indicating that the growth during M-phase is comparable to interphase when the short duration of M-phase is taken into consideration.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Growth during M-phase is comparable to interphase when the short duration of M-phase is taken into consideration.
source: We show that animal cells grow approximately 10% of their total mass during M-phase (Figure 1), indicating that the growth during M-phase is comparable to interphase when the short duration of M-phase is taken into consideration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative duration and amount of growth in M-phase.

claim: The findings contradict the classical dogma that growth takes place primarily during interphase and not during M-phase.
source: This contradicts the classical dogma that growth takes place primarily during interphase and not during M-phase.
evidence: This is a statement about how the findings relate to previous understanding.

claim: Mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dynamic.
source: Our single-cell measurements show that mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dynamic (Figure 2), dependent on mitotic stage (Figure 5), conserved across a variety of animal cell types grown in suspension (Figure 2) and reflected in protein synthesis rates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of observations from Figure 2.

claim: Mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dependent on mitotic stage.
source: Our single-cell measurements show that mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dynamic (Figure 2), dependent on mitotic stage (Figure 5), conserved across a variety of animal cell types grown in suspension (Figure 2) and reflected in protein synthesis rates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of observations from Figure 5.

claim: Mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is conserved across a variety of animal cell types grown in suspension.
source: Our single-cell measurements show that mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dynamic (Figure 2), dependent on mitotic stage (Figure 5), conserved across a variety of animal cell types grown in suspension (Figure 2) and reflected in protein synthesis rates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of observations from Figure 2 showing multiple cell types.

claim: Mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is reflected in protein synthesis rates.
source: Our single-cell measurements show that mass accumulation behavior during mitosis is dynamic (Figure 2), dependent on mitotic stage (Figure 5), conserved across a variety of animal cell types grown in suspension (Figure 2) and reflected in protein synthesis rates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of observations from Figure 3.

claim: Growth is only stopped for a short duration in mitosis, as cells approach the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: Importantly, growth is only stopped for a short duration in mitosis, as cells approach the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, and growth recovers in late cytokinesis after anaphase.
evidence: This is a summary of the dynamic growth behavior observed during mitosis.

claim: Growth recovers in late cytokinesis after anaphase.
source: Importantly, growth is only stopped for a short duration in mitosis, as cells approach the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, and growth recovers in late cytokinesis after anaphase.
evidence: This is a summary of the dynamic growth behavior observed during mitosis.

claim: Most studies on translation and growth signaling during mitosis use cell-population-based experimental approaches that require population enrichment for mitotic cells.
source: Most studies on translation and growth signaling during mitosis use cell-population-based experimental approaches that require population enrichment for mitotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement about common experimental approaches in the field.

claim: Population enrichment for mitotic cells is commonly achieved by mitotic blockades, which result in growth inhibition.
source: This is commonly achieved by mitotic blockades, which result in growth inhibition (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the observations in Figure 4 showing that mitotic arrests inhibit growth.

claim: Mitotic shake-off only enriches for the small subset of mitotic cells that are temporarily not growing (i.e. metaphase and anaphase cells).
source: Alternatively, mitotic cells can be collected with mitotic shake-off. However, this only enriches for the small subset of mitotic cells that are temporarily not growing (i.e. metaphase and anaphase cells).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only metaphase/anaphase cells have low growth rates.

claim: Many controversial reports regarding translational control during mitosis can be explained by experimental approaches.
source: Thus, many of the controversial reports regarding translational control during mitosis can be explained by experimental approaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion about how experimental methods may have led to conflicting results in the literature.

claim: The tight and conserved coordination between growth rates and mitotic stages suggests that mitotic growth control is important for cell division.
source: Conceptually, the tight and conserved coordination between growth rates and mitotic stages suggests that mitotic growth control is important for cell division.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the conservation of growth dynamics.

claim: Prioritization of energy away from ATP consuming macromolecule synthesis and towards mechanical reorganization of the cell could explain the reduction in mitotic protein synthesis rates.
source: It has been thought that prioritization of energy away from the ATP consuming macromolecule synthesis and towards mechanical reorganization of the cell could explain the reduction in mitotic protein synthesis rates (Kronja and Orr-Weaver, 2011; Sivan and Elroy-Stein, 2008; White-Gilbertson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Growth is stopped when the physical separation of daughter cells takes place.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that growth is stopped when the physical separation of daughter cells takes place (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on observations from Figure 2.

claim: There is no direct evidence that cell division would increase the energetic needs of a cell to a point where growth could not persist.
source: Yet, there is no direct evidence that cell division would increase the energetic needs of a cell to a point where growth could not persist, and the inhibition of growth may therefore be due to other reasons.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of evidence for a particular hypothesis.

claim: The inhibition of growth may protect cells from harmfully excessive cell growth during prolonged mitosis.
source: For example, the inhibition of growth may protect cells from harmfully excessive cell growth during prolonged mitosis (Miettinen and Björklund, 2016; Miettinen et al., 2017; Neurohr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous work (Miettinen and Björklund, 2016; Miettinen et al., 2017; Neurohr et al., 2019).

claim: A complete growth inhibition for the duration of M-phase would result in loss of short-lived proteins needed for mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: A complete growth inhibition for the duration of M-phase would result in loss of short-lived proteins needed for mitosis and cytokinesis (White-Gilbertson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature cited in the manuscript (White-Gilbertson et al., 2009).

claim: Growth is not inhibited during prophase or late cytokinesis, suggesting that short-lived proteins can be produced immediately prior to and after anaphase.
source: Consistently, we observe that growth is not inhibited during prophase or late cytokinesis, suggesting that short-lived proteins, such as survivin (White-Gilbertson et al., 2009), can be produced immediately prior to and after anaphase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that growth continues in prophase and late cytokinesis.

claim: CDK1 remains active until metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: Indeed, CDK1 remains active until metaphase-to-anaphase transition (Gavet and Pines, 2010), whereas mass accumulation rates begin to decay in late prometaphase and metaphase, indicating that CDK1 alone cannot fully explain the observed mass accumulation dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gavet and Pines, 2010.

claim: CDK1 alone cannot fully explain the observed mass accumulation dynamics.
source: Indeed, CDK1 remains active until metaphase-to-anaphase transition (Gavet and Pines, 2010), whereas mass accumulation rates begin to decay in late prometaphase and metaphase, indicating that CDK1 alone cannot fully explain the observed mass accumulation dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing mismatch between CDK1 activity and MAR reduction.

claim: Mitotic growth may be dependent on the time that cells have spent in mitosis, as growth can be limited by reduced chromatin accessibility and consequently reduced transcription.
source: Mitotic growth may be dependent on the time that cells have spent in mitosis, as growth can be limited by the reduced chromatin accessibility and consequently reduced transcription.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about a mechanism for growth reduction during mitosis.

claim: The gradual growth reduction during mitotic arrests is consistent with growth being limited by reduced chromatin accessibility.
source: This is consistent with the gradual growth reduction we observe during mitotic arrests (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observation in Figure 4 to the hypothesis about chromatin accessibility.

claim: Most mRNAs have long half-lives.
source: However, considering the long half-life of most mRNAs (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011), and the observations that mRNA levels do not decline during mitosis (Novais-Cruz et al., 2018; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), limited chromatin accessibility does not explain why protein synthesis would be reduced in the absence of mitotic arrests.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schwanhäusser et al., 2011.

claim: mRNA levels do not decline during mitosis.
source: However, considering the long half-life of most mRNAs (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011), and the observations that mRNA levels do not decline during mitosis (Novais-Cruz et al., 2018; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), limited chromatin accessibility does not explain why protein synthesis would be reduced in the absence of mitotic arrests.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Novais-Cruz et al., 2018 and Tanenbaum et al., 2015.

claim: Limited chromatin accessibility does not explain why protein synthesis would be reduced in the absence of mitotic arrests.
source: However, considering the long half-life of most mRNAs (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011), and the observations that mRNA levels do not decline during mitosis (Novais-Cruz et al., 2018; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), limited chromatin accessibility does not explain why protein synthesis would be reduced in the absence of mitotic arrests.
evidence: This is an inference based on mRNA stability and levels during mitosis.

claim: Normal mitotic progression results in more radical reduction in mass accumulation than what is observed in prometaphase arrested cells.
source: Furthermore, our results also show that normal mitotic progression results in more radical reduction in mass accumulation than what is observed in prometaphase arrested cells (Figure 5), indicating that there are also other mechanism(s) that radically reduce mass accumulation around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is based on comparisons shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are other mechanism(s) that radically reduce mass accumulation around metaphase-to-anaphase transition beyond time-dependent effects.
source: Furthermore, our results also show that normal mitotic progression results in more radical reduction in mass accumulation than what is observed in prometaphase arrested cells (Figure 5), indicating that there are also other mechanism(s) that radically reduce mass accumulation around metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of arrested and normally progressing cells.

claim: Cell mass accumulation reflects the flux of components, such as nutrients, in and out of the cell.
source: Cell mass accumulation reflects the flux of components, such as nutrients, in and out of the cell.
evidence: This is a statement about what mass accumulation measurements represent.

claim: The mechanism(s) controlling mass accumulation around metaphase-to-anaphase transition must either block cells from taking up nutrients or expel cellular components.
source: Because we observe that mass accumulation fully stops during anaphase, or even becomes negative in some cell types, the mechanism(s) controlling mass accumulation around metaphase-to-anaphase transition must either block the cells from taking up nutrients or even expel cellular components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of zero or negative mass accumulation.

claim: Cells can maintain translation even in the absence of nutrient uptake by degrading proteins and recycling the components.
source: Yet, this does not necessarily mean that protein synthesis comes to a complete stop, as cells can maintain translation even in the absence of nutrient uptake by degrading proteins and recycling the components (Son et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Son et al., 2015b.

claim: Prolonged mitotic arrests result in near zero mass accumulation although ~25% of the protein synthesis rate persists.
source: In fact, prolonged mitotic arrests resulted in near zero mass accumulation although ~25% of the protein synthesis rate persisted (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on observations from Figure 4.

claim: Around metaphase-to-anaphase transition, cells largely stop nutrient uptake but maintain low level of protein synthesis by recycling amino acids.
source: We therefore hypothesize that around metaphase-to-anaphase transition, where the anaphase-promoting complex drives protein degradation, cells largely stop nutrient uptake but maintain low level of protein synthesis by recycling amino acids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observations of mass accumulation and protein synthesis.

claim: Reducing CDK1 activity results in reduced growth in daughter cells.
source: We also observed that reducing CDK1 activity results in reduced growth in daughter cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on observations from Figure 7.

claim: CDK1-driven translation of growth components during mitosis may be required to 'jump-start' growth in newborn cells.
source: This may be explained by CDK1-driven translation of growth components during mitosis, such as ribosomal proteins, that are required to 'jump-start' growth in the newborn cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the daughter cell growth phenotype.

claim: Several studies have suggested that transcription and translation of growth-related genes are prioritized during mitosis.
source: Consistently, several studies have suggested that transcription and translation of growth-related genes are prioritized during mitosis (Aviner et al., 2017; Palozola et al., 2017; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aviner et al., 2017; Palozola et al., 2017; Park et al., 2016.

claim: CDK1 coordinates cell division and optimizes mitotic translation to promote immediate daughter cell growth.
source: These results imply that CDK1 does not only coordinate cell division, but also optimizes mitotic translation to promote immediate daughter cell growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of CDK1's effects on mitotic and daughter cell growth.

claim: The active mitotic translation of growth promoting components remains controversial.
source: However, it should be noted that the active mitotic translation of growth promoting components remains controversial (Stumpf et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), CDK1 inhibition may reduce daughter cell growth independently of mitotic growth, and the physiological significance of mitotic translational control in vivo remains unexplored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stumpf et al., 2013 and Tanenbaum et al., 2015.

claim: CDK1 inhibition may reduce daughter cell growth independently of mitotic growth.
source: However, it should be noted that the active mitotic translation of growth promoting components remains controversial (Stumpf et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), CDK1 inhibition may reduce daughter cell growth independently of mitotic growth, and the physiological significance of mitotic translational control in vivo remains unexplored.
evidence: This is a caveat about alternative interpretations of the data.

claim: The physiological significance of mitotic translational control in vivo remains unexplored.
source: However, it should be noted that the active mitotic translation of growth promoting components remains controversial (Stumpf et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2015), CDK1 inhibition may reduce daughter cell growth independently of mitotic growth, and the physiological significance of mitotic translational control in vivo remains unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about what remains unknown in the field.

claim: Mitotic arrests block cell growth.
source: Finally, our observations that mitotic arrests block cell growth have implications for antimitotic cancer chemotherapy.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the manuscript.

claim: Vincristine and Vinblastine stop cell growth when used in concentrations lower than those measured in patient plasma.
source: We observed that the vinca alkaloids Vincristine and Vinblastine, both commonly used to treat lymphomas, stop cell growth when used in concentrations lower than those measured in patient plasma (Florian and Mitchison, 2016).
evidence: This is based on observations from the manuscript and comparison to clinical concentrations cited from Florian and Mitchison, 2016.

claim: Mitotic growth arrest may contribute to the induction of mitotic catastrophe and the efficacy of antimitotic chemotherapies.
source: This mitotic growth arrest may contribute to the induction of mitotic catastrophe and the efficacy of antimitotic chemotherapies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the findings for cancer therapy.
